title: Good and Bad Bishops
subtitle: Your pawns decide whether your bishop is a piece or a spectator.
goals: Tell a good bishop from a bad one instantly
Place pawns off your bishop's colour
Rescue a bad bishop by re-routing it

steps.say: A 'bad' bishop is not a weaker piece — it is a bishop trapped behind its OWN pawns. Look at Black's bishop on e6: his pawns sit on d5 and c6, light squares, exactly where the bishop wants to go. Now look at yours on e3: your pawns are on dark... no, on c5 and d4 — also dark. Whichever bishop has fewer of its own pawns in the way is the good one, and the whole plan of the position follows from that single judgment.

steps.prompt: Black's bishop is hemmed in by his own pawns on c6 and d5. Activate YOUR bishop on the free diagonal!
hints: Your bishop wants a diagonal that your own pawns don't block. The kingside dark squares are wide open.
Bf4 takes the b8–h2 diagonal, where nothing of yours stands in the way.

line.say: Your bishop breathes; his does not. That asymmetry — one bishop with open diagonals, one staring at its own pawn chain — is worth more than a pawn in the long run, and it decides the plan: trade rooks, reach an endgame, and win with the better minor piece.

rejections.say: Careful: this puts another pawn on a dark square, the same colour as your bishop — the first step toward making it bad. Keep YOUR pawns off your bishop's colour.
Passive: from d2 the bishop looks at its own pawn on d4. Every bishop move should ask 'is this diagonal open?', and this one isn't.

steps.wrongSay: Put your bishop on a diagonal your own pawns don't block.
steps.successSay: Good bishop, bad bishop — the difference is just which squares your pawns occupy.

steps.prompt: Now YOUR bishop is the bad one — your d3 and c4 pawns block it. Start the re-route!
hints: You can't move the pawns quickly, so move the bishop instead: find a route to the other side of your own pawn chain.
Bd2 heads for c3 or b4 — outside the chain, where it finally has a diagonal.

line.say: The re-route begins. A bad bishop is not a permanent condition — it's a placement problem. Two tempi spent walking the bishop around your own pawns will often be the best two moves in the position.

rejections.say: This fixes MORE pawns on dark squares, permanently entombing your bishop. When your bishop is bad, never add pawns to its colour — either move the pawns off it or re-route the bishop.
It looks active, but ...g5 or ...e5 kicks it and you've lost time. The healthy plan is the patient one: walk the bishop out via d2.

steps.wrongSay: Your own pawns block the bishop. Walk it around them.
steps.successSay: Re-route the bishop or move the pawns — a bad bishop is a problem you can always solve.

steps.say: The rule to carry into every game: **put your pawns on the opposite colour to your bishop.** It makes your bishop good, gives your pawns protection your bishop cannot provide anyway, and — when you have to choose which minor piece to keep — tells you instantly which one is actually working.
